This is a layout specimen, written solely to test the website. It is not an article by the site’s author and is never included in a production build.

Reading on a screen is an exercise in attention. A line of text needs enough room to carry a thought, but not so much that finding the next line becomes work. The space around a paragraph is part of its structure: a small pause before the next idea begins.

## The shape of a paragraph

A serif typeface gives each word a distinct texture. The curves, brackets, and small differences between letters make a page feel measured without making it feel formal. In this specimen, *italic text* and **a stronger emphasis** appear alongside the ordinary rhythm of a sentence.

The aim is consistency across devices. At a desk, the text stays within a comfortable reading width. On a phone, the margins become smaller, while the letters remain large enough to read. A long word like “internationalization” should fit without creating a horizontal scrollbar.

> Space is useful when it makes the relationship between two ideas easier to see.
>
> This is a sample quotation, not an attributed statement.

## A few practical details

1. Dates follow the language of the article: Oct 16, 2026.
2. Links remain recognizable in both themes. [Read the Japanese specimen](/writing/ja-typography/).
3. Inline code, such as `publishedAt`, uses the system’s monospace font.

### Writing across languages

Japanese phrases such as 「文章のための余白」 can appear within an English paragraph. The baseline and spacing should preserve the flow of the surrounding text. Numbers (0123456789), punctuation — including dashes — and parentheses deserve the same care as the letters themselves.

The final paragraph is a reminder that the website’s job is simple: give the writing a calm, legible place to exist. Everything else should earn its space on the page.
